newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Political struggles block Ukraine's reforms.
newsitem.headline: Political struggles block Ukraine's reforms.

text.p: For the third successive year, Ukraine is starting summer locked in a serious political conflict which could mean more delays for economic reforms.

President Leonid Kuchma threw down the gauntlet last week by proposing extending parliament's term by one year to March 1999 and urging deputies to use the extra time to adopt economic reforms they have been blocking.
Socialist Speaker Olexander Moroz and leading deputies rejected the extension, complaining that Kuchma was overstepping his powers provided by the constitution.
"The political struggle and all these rows hamper reforms. Reforms, in fact, have stopped," said Iryna Klymenko, head of the centre for economic analysis at the influential Den daily.
"I doubt that Kuchma's latest initiative will have any positive impact on speeding up economic reforms," she said.
Kuchma said he wanted to avert the risk of parliament's work getting bogged down by campaigning ahead of elections scheduled for March 1998, so he would extend the deputies' term by a year.
The scene is set for Ukraine's third political battle over the constitution in as many years.

In June last year, Kuchma, caught in a row with deputies, announced a referendum on the constitution. Parliament initally opposed the move but gave in and approved it after an exhausting 25-hour session which left some deputies in tears.
In June 1995, Kuchma announced a similar referendum but got involved in a row with parliament which led to a temporary accord granting him broad powers until the document was passed.
The current stand-off is based on a long list of disagreements between Kuchma and parliament.
Kuchma wants to reserve tax privileges for joint ventures but the parliament and government fear Ukrainian firms simply register themselves as joint ventures to avoid paying tax.
Parliament wants to pass a law giving it more power over the government. Kuchma opposes this.
Klymenko also noted that the president and parliament had ruled separately on privatisation.

"We have two privatisation programmes -- one drawn up by presidential decree, and another by parliamentary resolution. We also have two different legal acts on leasing, on division of collective farms and so on," she said.

As a measure of the gulf between Kuchma and parliament, deputies took six months to pass the 1997 budget -- a key condition to $2.5-3 billion loan from the International Monetary Fund which may now consider a smaller, interim stand-by deal.
Some Western observers say Ukraine is so heavily locked in political struggles that it has distracted itself from the more important job of carrying out political and economic reforms.
"Democracy has done more harm to Ukraine than Marx ever did. And that's sad," former British Foreign Secretary Geoffrey Howe said last month.
"It is a good example of a country that has so far failed to address significantly a group of problems which are almost unmanageable."
Howe said Ukrainian officials were taking the constitutional separation of power too seriously and paralysing their country's political system as a result.

"Of course, it's easier to carry out reforms with authoritarian rule. Look at the history of Chile and South Korea," Olexander Yemets, a centrist deputy and former deputy prime minister responsible for the constitution, said.
"It's a choice between an authoritarian regime where some people go to prison but reforms are quick, or democracy with slower reforms. Ukraine has made a choice."

Unlike neighbouring Russia, where a standoff between president and parliament was resolved by violence in 1993, Ukraine has avoided bloodshed in the transition to democracy after decades of communist rule.
But some observers say Kuchma sends conflicting signals, seeking links with European countries who have traditions of parliamentary democracy while adopting an authoritarian style.

"The problems lie in the Bolshevik tradition. Kuchma envies (Russian President Boris) Yeltsin who has far wider powers and openly fights the opposition," Iryna Pohorelova, editor of Political Chronicles daily bulletin, said.
"Kuchma declares an intention to integrate with Europe, dominated by parliamentary democracies, but he prefers the Russian and U.S. models with a strong presidency."
